slides.0.title: New York II: Long Island, the Hudson River and beyond
slides.0.subtitle: Ocean, river valley and lake-shore AVAs
slides.1.title: Long Island's three AVAs
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Structure
slides.1.highlights.0.content: The Hamptons (16 May 1985) and North Fork (10 October 1986) came first; the parent "Long Island" AVA followed only on 14 May 2001, covering Nassau and Suffolk counties and offshore islands
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Climate
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The Atlantic, Long Island Sound and Peconic Bay moderate temperatures and lengthen the growing season by up to a month over inland New York
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Louisa and Alex Hargrave planted Long Island's first commercial vinifera vineyard in Cutchogue, on a former potato farm
slides.1.content: Long Island's AVA order is counter-intuitive: the sub-AVAs came before the parent.
slides.2.title: North Fork versus the Hamptons
slides.2.highlights.0.title: North Fork
slides.2.highlights.0.content: About 3,000 acres across 27 vineyards and over 40 wineries; a 195–201 day growing season and about 44 inches of rain; the main soil is Haven-Riverhead sandy loam
slides.2.highlights.1.title: The Hamptons
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Faces the Atlantic, so cooler and foggier; a growing season of about 182 days against about 195 on the North Fork (1978–1983 data); more silt and loam, holding more water
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Varieties
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Merlot and Chardonnay dominate, with Cabernet Franc and Riesling significant; Long Island places no restrictions on permitted grapes
slides.2.content: The North Fork is warmer and sandier; the Hamptons are cooler and more moisture-retentive.
slides.3.title: The Hudson River, Lake Erie and the Niagara Escarpment
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Hudson River Region
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Approved 4 June 1982 as New York's first AVA; Brotherhood Winery, founded in 1839, is called the oldest continuously operating winery in North America; French hybrids (Baco Noir, Seyval Blanc) and cool-climate vinifera both matter
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Lake Erie
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Approved 21 October 1983, spanning New York, Pennsylvania and Ohio; over 42,000 acres, mostly Concord
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Niagara Escarpment
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Approved 7 September 2005; about 18,000 acres with about 400 planted, on a free-draining limestone ridge
slides.3.content: New York now has eleven AVAs; East Coast AVAs often cover hybrids and American varieties, not only vinifera.
